prompt: The section says the general-chemistry rule (at most two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins) is close but not entirely accurate. What is the true statement of the Pauli exclusion principle?

choices.text: ψ is antisymmetric to exchanging identical fermions
ψ is symmetric to exchanging identical fermions
choices.why: Symmetric is the rule for bosons. For identical fermions, such as electrons, the wavefunction must be antisymmetric.

choices.text: No two electrons may share a molecular orbital
choices.why: Two electrons can share an orbital if their spins differ. The true statement is about exchange: ψ must be antisymmetric for identical fermions.

choices.text: Electrons with equal spins must stay on different atoms
choices.why: The principle says nothing about atoms. It requires the wavefunction to be antisymmetric to exchanging identical fermions.

explanation: The true Pauli principle: wavefunctions must be antisymmetric with respect to exchange of identical fermions, and symmetric with respect to exchange of identical bosons. The general-chemistry rule follows from it.

prompt: What does the Pauli principle require of the wavefunction when two identical bosons are exchanged?

choices.text: It must be symmetric, unchanged by the swap
It must be antisymmetric, changing sign
choices.why: Changing sign is the rule for fermions, such as electrons. For identical bosons the wavefunction must be symmetric.

choices.text: It must become zero after the swap
choices.why: Exchanging identical bosons leaves their wavefunction as it was; it does not vanish.

choices.text: Nothing, since the principle covers only electrons
choices.why: The principle covers all identical particles: antisymmetric for fermions and symmetric for bosons.

explanation: Wavefunctions must be symmetric with respect to exchange of identical bosons and antisymmetric with respect to exchange of identical fermions.

prompt: Why are electrons classed as fermions?

choices.text: They have half-integer spin, 1/2
They have integer spin, 1
choices.why: Particles with integer spin are bosons. Electrons have spin 1/2, a half-integer, which makes them fermions.

choices.text: They carry a negative electric charge
choices.why: Charge doesn't decide the class; spin does. Electrons have half-integer spin, 1/2, so they are fermions.

choices.text: They always occupy molecular orbitals
choices.why: Being in an orbital doesn't make a particle a fermion. Fermions are particles with half-integer spin, and an electron's spin is 1/2.

explanation: A fermion is a particle with half-integer spin, and a boson is a particle with integer spin. Electrons have spin 1/2, so they are fermions, and their wavefunctions must be antisymmetric.

prompt: How does the section treat the Pauli exclusion principle itself?

choices.text: As a fact, accepted without proof
As a result derived from the Aufbau principle
choices.why: It's the other way around: the section shows that the Aufbau filling rule follows from the Pauli principle, which it takes as a fact.

choices.text: As a consequence of Hund's rule
choices.why: Hund's rule is a separate rule about unpaired electrons. The section states the Pauli principle as a fact that it does not try to prove.

choices.text: As an approximation that fails for molecules
choices.why: The Pauli principle holds for every system of identical fermions, molecules included. The section accepts it as a fact without proof.

explanation: The section takes the Pauli exclusion principle as a fact, without trying to prove it, and then uses it to restrict how electrons occupy molecular orbitals, just as in multielectron atoms.

prompt: In the Pauli exclusion principle, what does it mean for an electronic wavefunction to be antisymmetric?

choices.text: It changes sign when two electron labels are swapped
It is unchanged when two electron labels are swapped
choices.why: That describes a symmetric wavefunction, as required for bosons. For electrons the wavefunction must change sign: p̂_12|ψ⟩ = −|ψ⟩.

choices.text: It has a node halfway between the two nuclei
choices.why: That describes the shape of an antibonding orbital, not exchange symmetry. Antisymmetric means the sign flips when two electrons' labels are swapped.

choices.text: It has different values on the two atoms of a molecule
choices.why: That would describe a lopsided orbital. Antisymmetric is about exchanging electrons: swapping two labels must change the sign.

explanation: If we swap two electrons, that is, exchange their labels, an antisymmetric wavefunction must change sign: p̂_12|ψ⟩ = −|ψ⟩.

prompt: Why must the electronic wavefunction be antisymmetric to the exchange of any two of its electrons, not just certain pairs?

choices.text: All electrons are identical
All electrons in a molecule are paired
choices.why: Many molecules, such as O2, have unpaired electrons. The rule covers every pair because electrons are identical particles.

choices.text: All electrons occupy the same orbital
choices.why: Electrons spread over many orbitals. The rule covers every pair because all electrons are identical.

choices.text: All electrons in a molecule have spin α
choices.why: Electrons can have spin α or β. The rule covers every pair simply because all electrons are identical.

explanation: Because all electrons are identical, the Pauli exclusion principle requires the electronic wavefunction to be antisymmetric with respect to exchanging any of them.

prompt: The section writes each spin orbital as |ψσ⟩. What do ψ and σ depend on?

choices.text: ψ on spatial coordinates only, σ on spin only
ψ on spin only, σ on spatial coordinates only
choices.why: It's the reverse: ψ is the spatial orbital, such as 1σ, and σ is the spin function, α or β.

choices.text: Both depend on space and spin together
choices.why: A spin orbital is a product of two separate parts: ψ depends only on the spatial coordinates, and σ only on the spin.

choices.text: σ marks a σ orbital and ψ its spin
choices.why: Here σ is not the σ of a σ orbital; it stands for the spin function, α or β. ψ is the spatial part.

explanation: A spin orbital |ψσ⟩ is a product of a spatial function ψ, which depends only on the electron's position, and a spin function σ (α or β), which depends only on its spin.

prompt: In the section's general Slater determinant for a closed-shell molecule, each spatial orbital φ_1, φ_2, …, φ_(N/2) appears in two columns. Why twice?

choices.text: Once with spin α and once with spin β
Once for each atom of the diatomic molecule
choices.why: Each MO already spreads over both atoms. It appears twice because it holds two electrons, one with spin α and one with spin β.

choices.text: Once in bonding and once in antibonding form
choices.why: Bonding and antibonding orbitals are different spatial orbitals. Each φ appears twice because it holds one α and one β electron.

choices.text: To make the determinant equal zero
choices.why: Identical columns would make it zero, but these two columns differ in spin, one α and one β. That is what lets each orbital hold two electrons.

explanation: Each orbital can hold one electron of each spin, so in a closed shell every φ_i appears once multiplied by α and once by β. N electrons therefore fill N/2 spatial orbitals.

prompt: In the section's H2 product |1σ^1α^1⟩|1σ^2β^2⟩, what do the superscripts 1 and 2 refer to?

choices.text: The label (number) of the electron
The number of electrons in the orbital
choices.why: In configurations like (σ_1s)^2 a superscript counts electrons, but here it is the electron's label: electron 1 or electron 2.

choices.text: Powers to which the functions are raised
choices.why: Nothing is squared here. The superscripts label the electrons, 1 or 2, so the effect of swapping them can be followed.

choices.text: The energy level of the orbital
choices.why: The 1 in 1σ gives the orbital's place in the energy order. The superscripts give the electron's label, 1 or 2.

explanation: Here a superscript is the electron number: |1σ^1α^1⟩ means electron 1 is in orbital 1σ with spin α. Swapping the labels with p̂_12 tests whether the wavefunction is antisymmetric.

prompt: The section says it may group the spatial and spin parts of the H2 wavefunction into kets in whichever way is most convenient. Why is that allowed?

choices.text: Spatial and spin coordinates are independent
The spin parts are always equal to 1
choices.why: Spin functions are not numbers. The grouping is free because the spatial and spin coordinates are independent of one another.

choices.text: The electrons in H2 have no spin of their own
choices.why: H2's electrons do have spin, α and β. The grouping is free because spin and spatial coordinates are independent.

choices.text: H2 has only one occupied spatial orbital
choices.why: The grouping would be free with several orbitals too. What matters is that spatial and spin coordinates are independent.

explanation: Since the spatial and spin coordinates are independent of one another, the factors of a product of spin orbitals can be grouped into kets in whatever way is convenient.

prompt: Spin α has m_z = 1/2 and spin β has m_z = −1/2. In ground-state H2, one electron has spin α and the other spin β. What is the sum of their m_z values?
explanation: 1/2 + (−1/2) = 0. The two electrons in the 1σ orbital have opposite spin projections, which cancel.

prompt: The section applies p̂_12, which swaps the labels of electrons 1 and 2, to the simple product |1σ^1α^1⟩|1σ^2β^2⟩ for H2. What does it find?

choices.text: It does not change sign, so it fails
It changes sign, so it is acceptable
choices.why: Swapping the labels gives |1σ^2α^2⟩|1σ^1β^1⟩, which is not −|ψ⟩. The product fails the test, so a linear combination is needed.

choices.text: It becomes zero, so H2 cannot exist
choices.why: The swapped product is not zero; it just isn't −|ψ⟩. H2 is fine; only the way its wavefunction is written must change.

choices.text: Its energy changes, so it is unacceptable
choices.why: Swapping labels doesn't change the energy. The problem is symmetry: the product doesn't turn into −|ψ⟩, as the Pauli principle requires.

explanation: p̂_12 turns |1σ^1α^1⟩|1σ^2β^2⟩ into |1σ^2α^2⟩|1σ^1β^1⟩, which is not equal to −|ψ⟩. The simple product isn't antisymmetric, so it breaks the Pauli exclusion principle.

prompt: The antisymmetrized H2 wavefunction is (1/√2)(|1σ^1α^1 1σ^2β^2⟩ − |1σ^2α^2 1σ^1β^1⟩). Why are the two terms subtracted rather than added?

choices.text: So that swapping the electrons turns ψ into −ψ
Adding them would make the whole function zero
choices.why: Adding gives a nonzero function, but a symmetric one that the swap leaves unchanged. Subtracting makes the swap turn ψ into −ψ.

choices.text: Subtracting lowers the energy of the molecule
choices.why: The Hamiltonian has no spin terms, so the combination has the same energy as the simple product. The minus sign is there for antisymmetry.

choices.text: The second electron has a negative spin
choices.why: Spin β has m_z = −1/2, but that's not why the terms are subtracted. The minus sign makes the function change sign when the labels are swapped.

explanation: Swapping the labels exchanges the two terms. With a minus sign between them, the result is minus the original, so the wavefunction is antisymmetric, as the Pauli principle requires. With a plus sign it would be symmetric.

prompt: Why does the antisymmetrized H2 wavefunction have the same energy as the simple product |1σ^1α^1⟩|1σ^2β^2⟩?

choices.text: The Hamiltonian has no terms that depend on spin
Both functions are normalized
choices.why: Normalization fixes the size of a function, not its energy. The energies match because the Hamiltonian has no spin-dependent terms.

choices.text: Antisymmetry never affects the energy of any state
choices.why: That's too broad. Here the energy is unchanged because the Hamiltonian contains no terms that depend on spin.

choices.text: The minus sign cancels the extra term's energy
choices.why: Energies aren't canceled term by term like this. The energy is unchanged because the Hamiltonian has no terms that depend on spin.

explanation: Since the Hamiltonian contains no spin-dependent terms, recombining the spin parts doesn't change the energy. The antisymmetrized function has the same energy as the simple product, and it obeys the Pauli principle.

prompt: What does the antisymmetrized H2 wavefunction show about how the 1σ orbital is occupied?

choices.text: By electrons in a superposition of spin states
By electron 1 with spin α and electron 2 with spin β
choices.why: That fixed assignment is the simple product, which fails the antisymmetry test. In the antisymmetrized function both labelings appear.

choices.text: By two electrons with the same spin
choices.why: Two electrons with the same spin can't share an orbital. The occupancy mixes both ways of assigning α and β.

choices.text: By a single electron shared by both atoms
choices.why: H2 has two electrons in 1σ. Each is in a superposition of spin states, since both labelings appear in the wavefunction.

explanation: The orbital is not occupied by one definite α electron and one definite β electron, but by electrons in a superposition of spin states. In larger systems every orbital is occupied by a superposition of all the electrons in both spin states.

prompt: The exact antisymmetrized wavefunction is hard to picture. How does the section say electrons can still be thought of in most practical cases?

choices.text: Each localized in one orbital with one spin
As spread evenly over all the occupied orbitals
choices.why: That is closer to the exact, hard-to-picture view. In practice each electron can be thought of as sitting in one orbital with one spin.

choices.text: As having no definite spin at all
choices.why: In practice each electron can still be given one spin, α or β, in one particular orbital, as in an MO diagram.

choices.text: As unpaired, one electron per orbital
choices.why: Orbitals still hold two electrons of opposite spin. The practical picture is simply each electron in one orbital with one particular spin.

explanation: Although antisymmetrized wavefunctions mix all the electrons over all the occupied spin orbitals, in most practical cases the electrons can be thought of as localized in one particular orbital with one particular spin, as an MO diagram shows.

prompt: According to the section, a Slater determinant contains all of the possible ways of doing what?

choices.text: Assigning numbers (labels) to the electrons
Arranging the nuclei in the molecule
choices.why: The nuclei are held fixed. The determinant covers every way of assigning the labels 1, 2, 3, … to the electrons.

choices.text: Placing electrons in excited orbitals
choices.why: A single determinant uses one fixed set of occupied orbitals. It runs through every way of numbering the electrons among them.

choices.text: Choosing which atomic orbitals go into the LCAO
choices.why: The orbitals are chosen beforehand. The Slater determinant contains all the ways of assigning electron numbers to those orbitals.

explanation: Each row of the determinant uses a different choice of electron labels, so the determinant contains every possible way of numbering the electrons, with signs that make the result antisymmetric.

prompt: According to the section's notes on Slater determinants, what happens if two columns of a determinant are swapped?

choices.text: It changes sign, as the Pauli principle requires
It is unchanged, since only the column order changes
choices.why: A determinant changes sign when two columns are swapped. That sign change is exactly the antisymmetry the Pauli principle requires.

choices.text: It becomes zero, as if two electrons merged
choices.why: A determinant is zero when two columns are identical, not when two are swapped. Swapping changes the sign.

choices.text: Its value doubles, one for each swapped column
choices.why: The size stays the same; only the sign flips. That sign change is why the Slater determinant satisfies the exclusion principle.

explanation: Swapping two columns of any determinant changes its sign. That is why a Slater determinant automatically satisfies the exclusion principle.

prompt: Putting two electrons with the same spin in the same orbital would give a Slater determinant two identical columns. Which familiar rule does the section say follows from this?

choices.text: At most one electron of each spin per orbital
Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity
choices.why: Hund's rule is about orbitals of equal energy. A determinant with two identical columns is zero, so each orbital can hold only one electron of each spin.

choices.text: The octet rule for main-group atoms
choices.why: The octet rule comes from Lewis structures. A determinant with two identical columns is zero, which limits each orbital to one electron of each spin.

choices.text: All electron spins in a molecule must be paired
choices.why: Molecules can have unpaired electrons, as O2 does. The zero determinant only forbids two electrons with the same spin in the same orbital.

explanation: A determinant with two identical columns is zero, so such a wavefunction can't exist. Each orbital can therefore hold only one electron of each spin, which leads directly to the Aufbau principle: fill orbitals in order of energy, two electrons each.

prompt: Suppose both electrons of H2 were put in the same spin orbital, 1σα. The two columns of its Slater determinant would then be identical: at one pair of positions, the rows are (0.6, 0.6) and (0.3, 0.3). Using ad − bc for a 2 × 2 determinant with rows (a, b) and (c, d), and leaving out the constant 1/√2, what is the determinant's value?
explanation: ad − bc = 0.6 × 0.3 − 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.18 − 0.18 = 0. A determinant with two identical columns is always zero, so two electrons can't share one spin orbital.

prompt: According to the section, when is the wavefunction described by a Slater determinant normalized?

choices.text: When the orbitals that make it up are normalized
Only when the molecule has an even number of electrons
choices.why: Any number of electrons works. With its 1/√(N!) factor, the determinant is normalized whenever its individual orbitals are.

choices.text: Never; it must be normalized again afterward
choices.why: No extra step is needed. The determinant is normalized as long as its individual orbitals are normalized.

choices.text: Only when all its orbitals are bonding orbitals
choices.why: Bonding or antibonding doesn't matter. The determinant is normalized if each orbital in it is normalized.

explanation: The wavefunction described by a Slater determinant, with its factor 1/√(N!), is normalized if the individual orbitals that make it up are normalized.

prompt: According to the section, when are two Slater determinants orthogonal?

choices.text: When they differ in any single orbital
Only when they differ in every orbital
choices.why: Every orbital need not differ. One different orbital is already enough to make two Slater determinants orthogonal.

choices.text: When they have the same number of electrons
choices.why: Having the same number of electrons doesn't make them orthogonal. They are orthogonal if they differ in any single orbital.

choices.text: Never, since they describe the same molecule
choices.why: Determinants for the same molecule can be orthogonal, for example a ground state and an excited state that differ in one orbital.

explanation: Two Slater determinants are orthogonal if they differ in any single orbital. For example, the ground-state determinant and one with an electron moved to a higher orbital are orthogonal.

prompt: In the independent particle approximation, the energy of a Slater determinant is the sum of the orbital energies of all its electrons. A closed-shell molecule has two electrons in an MO at −25 eV and two in an MO at −15 eV. What is the energy of its Slater determinant, in eV?
explanation: Add one orbital energy per electron: 2 × (−25 eV) + 2 × (−15 eV) = −50 eV − 30 eV = −80 eV.

prompt: A Slater determinant for N electrons carries the factor 1/√(N!). Li2 has 6 electrons (3 from each Li atom). What is the factor for ground-state Li2? (Give it as a decimal.)
Given an MO diagram, which two rules does the section use to write the Slater determinant for the ground state of a closed-shell molecule?

choices.text: The Aufbau principle and the Pauli principle
Hund's rule and the Aufbau principle
choices.why: In a closed-shell molecule every occupied orbital holds a pair, so Hund's rule has no role. The section uses the Aufbau and Pauli principles.

choices.text: The octet rule and the Pauli principle
choices.why: The octet rule belongs to Lewis structures, not MO diagrams. Electrons go in from lowest to highest energy (Aufbau), one of each spin per orbital (Pauli).

choices.text: The variational principle and Hund's first rule
choices.why: Neither is needed to write a closed-shell ground state. Fill orbitals from the bottom (Aufbau), with one electron of each spin per orbital (Pauli).

explanation: Each orbital can hold one electron of each spin (the Pauli principle), and electrons are placed into orbitals from lowest to highest energy (the Aufbau principle). The occupied spin orbitals then become the columns of the determinant.

prompt: A system with N electrons has an N × N Slater determinant. A nitrogen atom has 7 electrons. How many rows does the Slater determinant for ground-state N2 have?
explanation: N2 has 7 + 7 = 14 electrons, so its Slater determinant is 14 × 14: 14 rows and 14 columns.

prompt: From which functions can the Slater determinant procedure build a properly antisymmetrized electronic wavefunction?

choices.text: Any set of single-electron functions
Only exact eigenfunctions of the Hamiltonian
choices.why: Exact eigenfunctions aren't needed. The procedure works with any set of single-electron functions, such as approximate MOs.

choices.text: Only atomic orbitals, never molecular orbitals
choices.why: The section builds Slater determinants from molecular orbitals, such as H2's 1σ. Any set of single-electron functions will do.

choices.text: Only functions for an even number of electrons
choices.why: The section's general form assumes N is even for a closed shell, but the procedure itself works for any set of single-electron functions.

explanation: The Slater determinant is a standard procedure that generates an appropriately antisymmetrized electronic wavefunction from any set of single-electron functions, as it does for multielectron atoms.

prompt: What does the section conclude about the link between an MO diagram and the electronic wavefunction?

choices.text: It stands in for the Slater determinant it implies
It shows exactly where each electron is located in space
choices.why: An MO diagram shows which orbitals are occupied, not where the electrons are. It stands for the Slater determinant built from those orbitals.

choices.text: It is only a drawing, with no link to ψ
choices.why: The diagram is a real shorthand: it implies the Slater determinant used as the wavefunction in calculations.

choices.text: It replaces the need for the Pauli principle
choices.why: The diagram is filled using the Pauli principle. It then stands for the antisymmetrized Slater determinant.

explanation: An MO diagram can stand as an effective substitute for an electronic wavefunction: it is implied that the true wavefunction used in calculations comes from the Slater determinant described by the diagram.
